extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners (and patent applicants/attorneys as secondary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing and deciding whether a patent application's specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, including examiner procedures, burdens, and typical factual circumstances that give rise to written-description issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for determining evidence of possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of possession is a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include the level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention. Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to conclude the applicant was in possession is sufficient (citing Eli Lilly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Description obligation varies with art and invention scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention at issue, and with the scientific and technologic knowledge already in existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents and printed publications in the art should be relied upon to determine maturity and skill level. In mature technologies less detail may be required; in emerging or unpredictable technologies more evidence is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mature-technology exception for method/function disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: In most mature technologies, and where knowledge/skill in the art is high, a written description question should not be raised for claims present in the application when originally filed, even if the specification discloses only a method of making the invention and the function of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: microprocessor programming—disclosing a microprocessor capable of performing certain functions can be sufficient because one skilled in the art would know how to implement the necessary details (In re Hayes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater specificity required in unpredictable/emerging arts
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions in emerging and unpredictable technologies, or for inventions characterized by factors not reasonably predictable, more evidence is required to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and the function may not support a product claim (except product-by-process where the process was actually used to produce the product). Reduction to practice may be the only clear evidence of possession in such fields (citing Fiers, Amgen, Burroughs Wellcome).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial structure disclosure may be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization of the product may not be sufficient to evidence possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in molecular biology: conceiving a gene requires being able to define it to distinguish it from other materials (structure, method of preparation, physical/chemical properties); defining solely by a principal biological property (e.g., encoding EPO) is insufficient (Amgen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species claims must meet established tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Any claim to a species that does not meet the test described under at least one of (a), (b), or (c) must be rejected as lacking adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the specific (a)-(c) tests are referenced elsewhere in the guidance, the point is that a species claim must satisfy the applicable written-description test to avoid rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claim support options
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement for a claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species by actual reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or by disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure, physical/chemical properties), or by functional characteristics coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between function and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Eli Lilly and related case law for when such approaches are adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'representative number of species'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Representative number of species' means the species adequately described are representative of the entire genus; when substantial variation exists one must describe a sufficient variety of species to reflect the variation within the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of a single species supports a genus-only if the disclosure indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus (Enzo, Noelle v. Lederman). In unpredictable arts, one species usually will not suffice (In re Curtis, Eli Lilly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-species disclosures sometimes suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be situations where one species adequately supports a genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include cases where a skilled artisan would understand from the specification that the invention's scope does not depend on the particular species (Rasmussen, In re Herschler, In re Smythe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification cannot support expansive claims by describing only one embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification cannot always support expansive claim language merely by clearly describing one embodiment of the thing claimed; the issue is whether a person skilled in the art would understand the applicant invented, and was in possession of, the invention as broadly claimed (LizardTech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only one particular method/embodiment is taught, there must be evidence that the specification contemplated more generic methods or broader subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes a 'representative number' depends on predictability and skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination of what constitutes a representative number is an inverse function of the skill and knowledge in the art; satisfactory disclosure depends on whether one of skill would recognize that the applicant possessed the necessary common attributes of the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In unpredictable arts, adequate genus disclosure cannot generally be achieved by disclosing only one species. In predictable arts, fewer species may suffice; example in molecular biology where amino acid sequence disclosure can imply nucleic acid genus due to the known genetic code (In re Bell, In re Baird).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner initial burden when alleging lack of written description
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasoning to explain why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the original disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In making a rejection the examiner must set forth express findings of fact: (A) identify the claim limitation at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments supported by the application (see Rasmussen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant reply and re-evaluation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon reply by applicant, the examiner must re-determine the patentability of the claimed invention, including whether the written description requirement is satisfied, by reperforming the analysis in view of the whole record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the whole record demonstrates that the written description requirement is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection. If it still does not, fully respond to applicant's rebuttal and properly treat further showings; affidavits relevant to 112, para. 1 must be thoroughly analyzed and discussed if rejection is maintained (In re Alton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support requirement for new/amended claims and priority benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an explicit limitation in a claim is not present in the written description, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood that the description requires that limitation (Hyatt v. Boone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must include elements described as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must include all elements which applicant has described as essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the originally filed disclosure does not provide support for each claim limitation, or if an element described as essential is not claimed, a new or amended claim must be rejected under 35 U.S.C.112, para. 1, or a claim for priority must be denied (Johnson Worldwide, Gentry Gallery, Tronzo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete patentability determination and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must complete the patentability determination under all relevant statutory provisions of title 35 (including 101, 112, 102, 103) and clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and their bases in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review all proposed rejections and their bases to confirm correctness before imposing any rejection. Where possible, the Office action should offer helpful suggestions on how to overcome rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective standard for written description compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential question is whether the description clearly allows persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant must convey with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, he or she was in possession of the invention as now claimed (Vas-Cath, In re Gosteli, Ralston Purina v. Far-Mar-Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be demonstrated by actual reduction to practice, by showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession (Pfaff, Eli Lilly, Amgen, Lockwood).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-literal description and amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of the claim need not be described literally to satisfy the description requirement, but if a claim is amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed (a departure/addition/deletion), the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described in that application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a conclusion will result in rejection under 35 U.S.C.112, first paragraph, or denial of the benefit of the filing date of a previously filed application, as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical factual circumstances giving rise to written-description disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description issues most commonly arise in several circumstances: (I) amendments affecting a claim; (II) reliance on filing date of parent application under 35 U.S.C.120; (III) reliance on priority under 35 U.S.C.119; (IV) support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each circumstance raises the question whether the subject matter of the claim is supported in the application as filed; see cited cases (Wright; Tronzo; Scheiber; Ziegler; Fields v. Conover; Hyatt v. Boone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and nature of the inquiry (case-by-case factual issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry into whether the written description requirement is met must be determined on a case-by-case basis and is a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner bears an initial burden to present reasons/evidence; ultimate determinations rely on factual analysis of the specification and record (In re Wertheim).
